v.q: An ArrayList is full and add is called. Why is add still called O(1) amortised?
o: The array is copied only occasionally, and capacity grows geometrically
It copies the whole array on every single add
It inserts the new element at the front each time
It never needs to resize because lists are unbounded
v.w: Most adds are a single write; the O(n) copy happens rarely, so the cost averaged over many adds is constant.

v.q: Which statement about ArrayList growth is NOT true?
o: Every add copies the whole array
Capacity grows by a factor, not by one
Most adds are a single write
The occasional copy is O(n)
v.w: Copying on every add would make adds O(n). Growing geometrically spreads the copy cost over many adds.

v.q: Why is ArrayList usually faster than LinkedList for traversal in practice?
o: Its elements sit contiguously in memory, so the CPU cache is used well
Every ArrayList operation is O(1)
LinkedList cannot store more than a few elements
ArrayList nodes hold pointers to the next element
v.w: Contiguous elements mean fewer cache misses and less memory per element. LinkedList nodes are scattered objects with extra pointers.

v.q: For a list you mostly read by index, which is the better choice?
o: ArrayList
LinkedList
Both are the same
Stack
v.w: ArrayList has O(1) index access. LinkedList must walk from one end.

v.q: A HashMap key's hashCode changes after it was stored. What happens on lookup?
o: The entry may not be found, because the lookup goes to a different bucket
The map automatically moves the entry to the right bucket
The lookup always throws an exception
Nothing changes, because equals decides the bucket
v.w: The bucket was chosen from the old hash code. Keys should be immutable, or at least their hash must not change while stored.

v.q: Which key makes a good HashMap key?
o: An immutable object with equals and hashCode implemented together
A mutable list whose contents change
An object that overrides only equals
An object whose hashCode returns a random number
v.w: The hash must not change while the key is stored, and equal keys must have equal hash codes.

v.q: What does a plain binary search tree degrade into when keys are inserted in sorted order?
o: A chain like a linked list, with O(n) operations
A perfectly balanced tree with O(log n) operations
A hash table with O(1) operations
A heap with the smallest value on top
v.w: Each new key goes to the right, so the height equals the number of nodes. Red-black trees such as TreeMap rotate to prevent this.

v.q: Which statement about a self-balancing tree such as a red-black tree is NOT true?
o: It stays balanced without any extra work on insert
TreeMap uses a red-black tree
Operations stay O(log n)
It uses rotations to keep the height small
v.w: Rotations and recolouring after inserts and deletes are exactly the extra work that keeps the tree balanced.

v.q: Which structure always gives you the smallest element next, in O(log n) per removal?
o: A min-heap, as in PriorityQueue
A HashMap
An ArrayList kept in insertion order
A queue
v.w: A heap guarantees only the top element, which makes it ideal for top-k and scheduling, but it is not fully sorted.

v.q: You need the 10 largest values from a stream of millions. Which structure is the best fit?
o: A min-heap of size 10
A sorted array of every value
A HashSet of every value
A linked list in arrival order
v.w: Keep ten values in a min-heap and drop the smallest when a bigger one arrives. That costs O(log 10) per item.

v.q: Which traversal finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
o: Breadth-first search with a queue
Depth-first search with a stack
In-order traversal of a tree
Binary search on the node ids
v.w: BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches a node is by the fewest edges. DFS does not guarantee this.

v.q: Which goal is NOT a good fit for breadth-first search?
o: A stack
A queue
A sorted set
A priority queue
v.w: BFS keeps a whole frontier in memory. DFS needs only the current path, so it uses less memory on deep graphs.

v.q: Which Java class is the best choice for both a stack and a queue?
o: ArrayDeque
Stack
Vector
LinkedList
v.w: ArrayDeque has O(1) operations at both ends and no synchronisation overhead; Stack and Vector are legacy synchronised classes.

v.q: Which structure gives O(1) push and pop at the same end?
o: A stack
A queue
A sorted set
A priority queue
v.w: A stack is last in, first out. A queue removes from the opposite end and a priority queue removes the smallest.

v.q: How can you build an LRU cache with O(1) get and put?
o: A hash map combined with a doubly linked list ordered by recent use
A sorted array searched with binary search
A single ArrayList that is scanned on every get
A TreeMap keyed by the value stored
v.w: The map gives O(1) lookup and the list moves an entry to the front and evicts from the tail in O(1). LinkedHashMap with access order does this.

v.q: Which statement about LinkedHashMap with access order is NOT true?
o: It sorts entries by key
It can evict the least recently used entry
Reading an entry moves it to the end
It keeps a linked list through the entries
v.w: It orders by access, not by key. TreeMap is the one sorted by key.
